php-echo-superglobal-xss.problem: You echo a value from $_GET, $_POST, $_REQUEST, or $_COOKIE directly into the page. PHP does not escape it, so any HTML or JavaScript an attacker puts in the URL or form is rendered as part of the page.
php-echo-superglobal-xss.impact: Reflected XSS: an attacker can steal session cookies, deface the page, or run actions in the user's browser as if they came from your site.
php-echo-superglobal-xss.fix: Wrap the value with htmlspecialchars($_GET['x'], ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8') before echoing, or use a templating engine (Twig, Blade) that auto-escapes.

php-echo-interp-superglobal.problem: An echo string interpolates $_GET, $_POST, or another superglobal directly inside a double-quoted string. The raw user value is embedded into the HTML output without escaping.
php-echo-interp-superglobal.impact: Reflected XSS, same as a direct echo of the superglobal — attackers can inject script and take over user sessions.
php-echo-interp-superglobal.fix: Pull the value into a sanitized local variable first: $name = htmlspecialchars($_GET['name'], ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8'); echo "Hello $name";.

php-eval-call.problem: eval() runs the string it receives as PHP source. If any part of that string can be influenced by an HTTP request, the user controls the code path the server executes.
php-eval-call.impact: Full remote code execution: read any file the PHP user can read, open outbound connections, drop a webshell.
php-eval-call.fix: Eliminate eval(). Use a real parser, a config file, or call_user_func() against a small allowlist of named callables.

php-shell-exec-call.problem: shell_exec() runs its argument through the operating-system shell. Special characters in the argument (;, |, &&, backticks) are interpreted by the shell.
php-shell-exec-call.impact: Command injection — an attacker can run arbitrary commands as the web server user and read or modify any file it can touch.
php-shell-exec-call.fix: Avoid the shell. Use proc_open() with an argv array, or pass each argument through escapeshellarg() before concatenating.

php-exec-call.problem: exec() executes a command through the shell. User-supplied content in the command string is parsed by the shell, not as a literal argument.
php-exec-call.impact: Command injection leading to remote code execution under the web server account.
php-exec-call.fix: Either drop shell execution entirely or wrap each variable argument with escapeshellarg(). Better: switch to proc_open() with an argv array.

php-system-call.problem: system() runs a shell command and prints its output. A variable $CMD typically contains user-supplied data that the shell will parse.
php-system-call.impact: Command injection: the attacker can read /etc, exfiltrate database credentials, or spawn a reverse shell.
php-system-call.fix: Use proc_open() with separate arguments. If you must use system(), validate $CMD against a strict allowlist before the call.

php-passthru-call.problem: passthru() runs a shell command and streams binary output to the browser. Any unescaped variable in the command line is interpreted by the shell.
php-passthru-call.impact: Command injection on the server, with the added side-effect that response bodies become unpredictable.
php-passthru-call.fix: Replace passthru() with proc_open() and read the process stdout in PHP. Validate every variable argument before use.

php-include-variable.problem: include/require with a variable file path lets the caller pick which PHP file the server will execute. If the variable reaches the request, the attacker chooses the path.
php-include-variable.impact: Local File Inclusion (LFI) leading to source disclosure, log poisoning, or RCE. With allow_url_include enabled it becomes Remote File Inclusion.
php-include-variable.fix: Build a switch/whitelist that maps known IDs to fixed file paths. Never concatenate $_GET/$_POST into an include path.

php-include-once-variable.problem: include_once/require_once with a variable file path has the same risk as include with a variable path — the include target is dynamic.
php-include-once-variable.impact: LFI/RFI: attacker can disclose source, execute arbitrary PHP files, or in some configurations include remote URLs.
php-include-once-variable.fix: Map user input to a fixed set of files via a switch or array lookup. Reject anything not in the allowlist.

php-unserialize-call.problem: unserialize() reconstructs PHP objects from a string. Through magic methods (__wakeup, __destruct), specially crafted payloads can trigger code paths in any class the application has loaded.
php-unserialize-call.impact: Object-injection attacks leading to remote code execution, file deletion, or authentication bypass.
php-unserialize-call.fix: Use json_decode() / json_encode() for untrusted data. If unserialize() is unavoidable, pass the allowed_classes option restricting it to a tiny allowlist.

php-mysqli-query-concat.problem: The SQL string is built by concatenating a variable. If $V comes from the request, the database parses attacker SQL as part of the query.
php-mysqli-query-concat.impact: SQL injection: full read/write access to the database, including credential dumps, data tampering, and in some setups RCE via INTO OUTFILE.

php-mysql-query-deprecated.problem: The legacy ext/mysql functions (mysql_query, mysql_connect, ...) were removed in PHP 7. They never offered real parameterized queries.
php-mysql-query-deprecated.impact: Code that runs on PHP 7+ will simply error out, and any SQL built around it is almost always concatenated and SQL-injectable.
php-mysql-query-deprecated.fix: Migrate to mysqli or PDO with prepared statements and bound parameters.

php-weak-hash-md5.problem: md5() is fast and collision-broken. Using it for passwords or security tokens means a modern GPU can recover passwords in minutes from a stolen hash.
php-weak-hash-md5.impact: Stolen hashes are effectively cleartext passwords; reused passwords leak to other services.
php-weak-hash-md5.fix: For passwords use password_hash($pwd, PASSWORD_DEFAULT) and password_verify(). For tokens use random_bytes(32) and store the hex/base64. md5() is fine only for non-security checksums.

php-weak-hash-sha1.problem: sha1() has documented collisions and is too fast to resist brute-force on a stolen password database.
php-weak-hash-sha1.impact: Same risk as md5 when used for credentials: hashes are crackable, integrity checks can be forged.
php-weak-hash-sha1.fix: Use password_hash() for passwords. For data integrity use hash('sha256', $data) or hash_hmac('sha256', $data, $key).

php-hardcoded-password.problem: A variable named like password / secret / apiKey / token is initialized with a literal string. Anyone with read access to the repo or the deployed file gets the credential.
php-hardcoded-password.impact: Credential leak: the secret ends up in git history, container images, and developer machines. Rotating it requires a code change.
php-hardcoded-password.fix: Read the value from getenv('API_KEY') or a secrets manager. Keep the literal only in .env files that are git-ignored.

php-curl-ssl-verify-false.problem: Setting CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER to false disables the TLS certificate check. The cURL handle will accept any certificate, including self-signed or attacker-controlled ones.
php-curl-ssl-verify-false.impact: Man-in-the-middle: anyone on the network path can intercept and modify the supposedly-secure request, stealing tokens or injecting responses.
php-curl-ssl-verify-false.fix: Leave the option at its default (true). If a corporate CA is in use, point CURLOPT_CAINFO at the right bundle instead of disabling verification.

php-error-reporting-display-prod.problem: ini_set('display_errors', '1') tells PHP to render warnings and stack traces in the HTTP response. In production this leaks file paths, library versions, and SQL fragments.
php-error-reporting-display-prod.impact: Information disclosure that helps attackers craft targeted exploits, and confusing UX for normal users.
php-error-reporting-display-prod.fix: Set display_errors to '0' in production and rely on log_errors / error_log() instead. Use a frontend that shows a generic 5xx page.

php-empty-catch.problem: The catch block has no statements. The exception is silently discarded — no log entry, no rethrow, no fallback.
php-empty-catch.impact: Bugs disappear: a failed payment looks successful, a missing file is treated like an empty one. Debugging future issues becomes guesswork.
php-empty-catch.fix: Log the exception at minimum (error_log($e->getMessage())), then either rethrow or apply an explicit fallback. Never use catch as a way to suppress errors.

php-loose-equality.problem: PHP's == operator performs type juggling: '0' == 'abc' is true on PHP 7, 0 == 'abc' was true before PHP 8, '1e2' == '100' is always true. Comparisons rarely match the developer's intuition.
php-loose-equality.impact: Authentication bypasses (token == 0), wrong branches taken, hard-to-find logic bugs.
php-loose-equality.fix: Use === and !== to compare both value and type. If you really need loose coercion, cast explicitly: (string)$a === (string)$b.

php-todo-comment.problem: A TODO or FIXME comment is left in the source. It signals known incomplete work but has no owner or deadline attached.
php-todo-comment.impact: The note rots in the codebase, new contributors assume the comment is current, and the underlying issue never gets fixed.
php-todo-comment.fix: Open a ticket in the issue tracker with the context, link it from the comment, or just complete the work before merging.

php-var-dump-prod.problem: var_dump() / print_r() write the contents of a variable directly to the response. Often a debugging leftover that ships with the release.
php-var-dump-prod.impact: Leaks internal state — database rows, session data, config — to anyone who can hit the page, breaks page layout, and confuses users.
php-var-dump-prod.fix: Remove debug calls before committing, or route them through error_log() / a proper debug logger guarded by an environment flag.

php-file-get-contents-url.problem: file_get_contents() with a variable URL means the server fetches whatever address the caller chooses. If the variable reaches user input, the attacker controls the destination.
php-file-get-contents-url.impact: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF): the attacker can hit internal services (169.254.169.254, internal Redis, intranet admin pages) using your server's network credentials.
php-file-get-contents-url.fix: Parse the URL with parse_url(), enforce a scheme allowlist (https only), and validate the host against a domain allowlist before the request.
